keyQuotes: Freshness is the currency of a World Cup. The teams that preserve it best may ultimately give themselves the greatest chance of success.
The team around the team... is maybe sometimes even more important than the guys there on the pitch.
You know who is the best player? The satisfied player. The player that is satisfied, that is happy, is going to go out and give 120 per cent.

mainPoints.explanation: While jet lag from crossing time zones can be managed with arrival schedules, the repeated travel between matches, cities, and environments drains time for recovery, preparation, and routine.
mainPoints.point: Travel fatigue is the cumulative burden of repeated journeys, not just jet lag.

mainPoints.explanation: Muscle energy and dehydration may restore quickly, but muscle soreness and inflammation persist longer. Mental fatigue from sustained concentration and pressure has no clear recovery timeline and is harder to monitor.
mainPoints.point: Physical and mental fatigue recover at different rates and require different approaches.

mainPoints.explanation: Players like Rakitić and Mertesacker emphasize that a positive atmosphere and caring staff (the 'team around the team') provide the psychological and emotional freshness that fuels performance.
mainPoints.point: Team environment—trust, communication, and relationships—is more important than any single recovery protocol.

mainPoints.explanation: England returning to the same city after each match helps maintain time zone consistency and routine, but adds travel distance. The decision depends on team culture and individual preferences.
mainPoints.point: Fixed base camps can reduce the cognitive load of travel, but may not suit every team or player.

oneSentenceSummary: This article examines how World Cup teams manage travel fatigue, jet lag, sleep disruption, and accumulated physical and mental fatigue, arguing that freshness—both physical and psychological—is the key currency for deep tournament runs.
originalTitle: How World Cup teams cope with travel， lack of sleep and accumulated fatigue
summary: This article is part of The Athletic's World Cup performance series, written by performance expert Alan McCall. It focuses on the challenges of travel and accumulated fatigue as teams enter the knockout rounds. Drawing on interviews with players (Bacary Sagna, Ivan Rakitić, Per Mertesacker) and recovery specialists (Shona Halson, Darcy Norman, Anna West), the piece explains how jet lag, repeated travel, and disrupted sleep affect performance. It distinguishes between physical recovery (energy stores, muscle soreness) and mental fatigue, which is harder to measure and recover from. The author argues that preserving freshness requires not just logistics but also a supportive environment—trust, relationships, and communication. Examples include England's decision to return to a fixed base in Kansas City and Croatia's team atmosphere in 2018. The article concludes that the best plans cannot predict everything; human connection and adaptability are essential.
title: How World Cup teams cope with travel， lack of sleep and accumulated fatigue
